extracted.intended_audience: USPTO patent examiners and patent practitioners (applicants and patent attorneys)
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance for using affidavits/declarations under 37 CFR 1.131 to antedate references or activities and thereby overcome prior‑art or activity-based rejections. Covers effective reference dates, who may sign, formalities, special situations (joint publications, common ownership, genus/species issues), and form paragraph usage.

rubrics_metrics.name: Lost count in interference as prior art or subject to interference estoppel
rubrics_metrics.description: Where the subject matter corresponding to a lost count in an interference may be prior art under 35 U.S.C. 102(g) or barred to applicant by the doctrine of interference estoppel; however, exceptions exist (e.g., losing party may antedate if invention now claimed is not 'substantially the same'). A count lost based on the winner’s foreign priority date may not be prior art under 35 U.S.C. 102(g) as to the loser.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Cites In re Bandel; In re Kroekel; In re Deckler (res judicata/collateral estoppel); In re Zletz (loser may use 37 CFR 1.131 if invention not 'substantially the same'); In re McKellin (count lost on basis of winner’s foreign priority date is not prior art to loser). See MPEP §§2138.01–2138.02 for additional treatment. Note difference between estoppel (unpatentable to other party) and statutory prior art availability.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reference date to be overcome
rubrics_metrics.description: The date to be overcome under 37 CFR 1.131 is the effective date of the reference (i.e., the date on which the reference is available as prior art).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This is the controlling temporal benchmark for affidavits/declarations under 37 CFR 1.131; the effective date varies by type of reference (patent, publication, activity). See the following specific categories for how to determine effective date.

rubrics_metrics.name: Effective date for U.S. patents, U.S. patent application publications, and PCT/WIPO international publications
rubrics_metrics.description: U.S. patents, U.S. patent application publications, and WIPO publications of international applications are available as prior art under 35 U.S.C. 102(e) and the effective date used to be overcome is their effective U.S. filing date, not any foreign filing date to which they may be entitled under 35 U.S.C. 119(a).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: See MPEP §706.02(a), §706.02(f)(1), and §§2136–2136.03 for detailed discussion. In re Hilmer: effective date of a domestic patent as a reference is not the foreign filing date. When a U.S. patent/publication claims benefit of an earlier application, determine effective filing date under 35 U.S.C. 102(e) per MPEP guidance.

rubrics_metrics.name: Effective date for foreign patents
rubrics_metrics.description: The availability/date of a foreign patent as prior art is governed by the rules for foreign patents (see MPEP §2126–§2127).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Consult MPEP §§2126–2127 for how and when foreign patents are treated as prior art and what their effective dates are in the U.S. context.

rubrics_metrics.name: Effective date for printed publications
rubrics_metrics.description: A printed publication (including a published foreign patent application) is effective as of its publication date, not the date of receipt by the publisher.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: See MPEP §§2128–2128.02 for additional information about determining effective publication dates and evaluating printed-publication prior art.

rubrics_metrics.name: Effective date for activities (admissions, use, knowledge)
rubrics_metrics.description: Where the rejection relies on an activity (admission by applicant, evidence of use of the invention, knowledge by others, or examiner personal knowledge), the effective date of that activity is the date the activity was first known to have occurred.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: See MPEP §706.02(c) and §2133.03. Note statutory limitations in 37 CFR 1.131(a)(1) and 35 U.S.C. 104 that only acts occurring in this country or in a NAFTA or WTO member country may be relied on to establish a date of invention in certain contexts.

rubrics_metrics.name: Form paragraphs 7.57–7.64 for 37 CFR 1.131 responses (use and sequencing)
rubrics_metrics.description: Standard form paragraphs (7.57–7.64) are available for examiners to notify applicants whether an affidavit/declaration under 37 CFR 1.131 has been considered and whether it is effective or ineffective to overcome a reference.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Paragraph 7.57 is a heading indicating the affidavit/declaration has been considered but is ineffective and must be followed by one or more of paragraphs 7.58–7.63 or by a specific paragraph explaining the insufficiency. Bracketed placeholders must be filled in (e.g., insert 'affidavit' or 'declaration', filing dates, reference identity). Paragraph 7.64 is used when the affidavit/declaration is sufficient to overcome the reference. Use the appropriate succeeding paragraph(s) to state the ground (e.g., insufficient conception, lack of diligence, insufficient reduction to practice). See examiner notes in each form paragraph.

rubrics_metrics.name: ¶ 7.58 Ineffective — reference claims same invention
rubrics_metrics.description: Affidavit/declaration under 37 CFR 1.131 is inappropriate when the reference is a U.S. patent or U.S. patent application publication that claims the rejected invention (i.e., the reference is claiming the same patentable invention).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If the reference and the application are not commonly owned, the proper mechanism to overcome is to establish priority via interference proceedings (MPEP Chapter 2300). If commonly owned, the reference may be disqualified by an affidavit/declaration under 37 CFR 1.130. Affidavits filed improperly under 1.131 may be considered as filed under 1.132 to traverse the ground (see In re Facius). Use form paragraph sequencing consistent with 7.57 when responding to an affidavit submission.

rubrics_metrics.name: ¶ 7.59 Ineffective — insufficient evidence of reduction to practice before reference date
rubrics_metrics.description: The evidence submitted is insufficient to establish reduction to practice of the invention in this country or a NAFTA/WTO member country prior to the effective date of the reference.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This paragraph must be preceded by form paragraph 7.57. Examiner should provide an explanation of the lack of showing in the bracketed text. Distinguish this ground from insufficient conception (¶7.60) or lack of diligence (¶7.62).

rubrics_metrics.name: ¶ 7.60 Ineffective — insufficient evidence of conception
rubrics_metrics.description: The evidence submitted is insufficient to establish a conception of the invention prior to the effective date of the reference. Conception must be capable of proof (demonstrative evidence or complete disclosure to another) and is more than a vague idea; the means and their interaction must be comprehended.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Must be preceded by ¶7.57. If affidavit also fails to establish diligence or reduction to practice, follow with ¶7.62 and/or ¶7.63 as appropriate. If either diligence or reduction to practice is established, state that after this paragraph. Cite Mergenthaler v. Scudder for conception standard. Provide bracketed explanation of the deficiency.

rubrics_metrics.name: ¶ 7.62 Ineffective — diligence lacking
rubrics_metrics.description: The evidence is insufficient to establish diligence from a date prior to the date of reduction to practice of the reference to either a constructive reduction to practice or an actual reduction to practice.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Must be preceded by ¶7.57. If affidavit also fails conception, ¶7.61 must precede; if affiant establishes conception, add a statement to that effect. If affidavit also fails to establish an alleged reduction to practice prior to application filing date, follow with ¶7.63. Provide explanation of reasons for non-diligence in bracketed text. Note Ex parte Merz indicating diligence not required after reduction to practice.

rubrics_metrics.name: ¶ 7.63 Ineffective — insufficient evidence of actual reduction to practice
rubrics_metrics.description: The evidence submitted is insufficient to establish applicant’s alleged actual reduction to practice of the invention in this country or a NAFTA/WTO member country after the effective date of the reference.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Must be preceded by ¶7.57. Do not use this paragraph if alleged reduction to practice is prior to the effective date of the reference (use ¶7.59). If affidavit also fails to establish conception or diligence, include ¶7.61/¶7.62 before this paragraph. Explain the lack of showing in bracketed text.

rubrics_metrics.name: ¶ 7.64 Effective — affidavit/declaration suffices to overcome reference
rubrics_metrics.description: The affidavit/declaration filed under 37 CFR 1.131 is sufficient to overcome the named reference.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: In bracketed text insert whether affidavit or declaration, the filing date of the affidavit/declaration, and the identity of the reference. Use when the presented evidence establishes the required dates/possession to antedate the reference.

rubrics_metrics.name: Purpose of 37 CFR 1.131 vs 1.132 (when to use each)
rubrics_metrics.description: The purpose of a 37 CFR 1.131 affidavit/declaration is to overcome a prior-art rejection by proving applicant's invention date prior to the effective date of the reference or activity. Where appropriate, an applicant may instead use a 37 CFR 1.132 affidavit/declaration to prove that the subject matter relied upon in the reference or activity was applicant’s own invention or derived from applicant.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Affidavits under 1.131 establish invention dates; 1.132 is used to show derivation/common ownership or that the reference discloses applicant’s own work. Affidavits improperly filed under 1.131 may be treated as though filed under 1.132 (In re Facius). For rejections under 35 U.S.C. 103 based on references qualifying only under 102(f)/(g) or certain 102(e) contexts, showing common ownership or assignment at time of later invention may preclude the rejection (see MPEP §706.02(l)). See MPEP §716.10 for using 1.132 to traverse references.

rubrics_metrics.name: Joint patent or application publication to applicant and another
rubrics_metrics.description: When subject matter disclosed but not claimed in a patent or application publication filed jointly by applicant and another is later claimed by applicant, the joint patent/publication is a valid reference under 35 U.S.C. 102(a) or (e) unless overcome by an affidavit/declaration under 37 CFR 1.131 or an unequivocal 1.132 declaration by the co‑applicant establishing that the subject matter relied on was applicant’s invention.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: In re DeBaun cited. A disclaimer by the other patentee/applicant is not required but may be accepted by the examiner. Affidavits submitted under 1.131 to show applicant’s invention but more properly within 1.132 will be considered under 1.132 to traverse the rejection.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reference and application have common assignee — effect on affidavits
rubrics_metrics.description: Common ownership of the reference patent/publication and the application does not itself eliminate the need for an affidavit/declaration under 37 CFR 1.131 (or 1.132) unless a showing is made under 37 CFR 1.132 that the patentee derived the subject matter from the applicant.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Cites In re Frilette, Pierce v. Watson, In re Beck. However, where the rejection is applied under 35 U.S.C. 102(f)/103 or 102(g)/103 or under 102(e)/103 for post-November 29, 1999 filings, a showing that the invention was commonly owned or subject to an obligation of assignment at the time the later invention was made may preclude or overcome such a rejection (see MPEP §706.02(l) and (l)(1)).

rubrics_metrics.name: Reference is publication of applicant's own invention
rubrics_metrics.description: A rejection based on a publication (not a statutory bar) may be overcome by showing that the publication was by applicant or on applicant’s behalf; such a showing is not necessarily aimed at proving a date of invention in a foreign country (37 CFR 1.131 limitations).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use 37 CFR 1.132 affidavits/declarations to show that the reference is a publication of applicant’s own invention. See Ex parte Lemieux and Ex parte Powell. Note distinctions regarding acts occurring in this country versus foreign countries per 35 U.S.C. 104 and 37 CFR 1.131(a)(1). See MPEP §716.10.

rubrics_metrics.name: Co-authorship — applicant as co-author of cited publication
rubrics_metrics.description: Where applicant is one of the co-authors of a cited publication, applicant may overcome the rejection by filing an affidavit/declaration under 37 CFR 1.131 or by filing a specific affidavit/declaration under 37 CFR 1.132 establishing that the article describes applicant’s own work; an affidavit by applicant alone indicating sole inventorship and that others were working under direction can remove the publication as a reference under 35 U.S.C. 102(a).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Cites In re Katz. Examiner should accept an affidavit establishing applicant’s authorship/sole-inventor status when properly supported.

rubrics_metrics.name: Derivation (showing reference author derived from applicant)
rubrics_metrics.description: When unclaimed subject matter of a patent, application publication, or other publication is applicant’s own invention, the rejection (if not a statutory bar) may be removed by evidence that the patentee/author derived the knowledge from applicant and that applicant made the invention upon which the disclosure is based.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Cites In re Mathews and In re Facius. Such proof may justify disqualification of the reference or overcoming the rejection under appropriate rules (typically via 1.132 procedures).

rubrics_metrics.name: Activities applied against claims — remedies (antedate or show applicant performed activity)
rubrics_metrics.description: A rejection based on an activity showing the claimed invention was used or known prior to the filing date may be overcome by an affidavit/declaration under 37 CFR 1.131 establishing a date of invention prior to the activity, or by a specific affidavit/declaration under 37 CFR 1.132 showing that the activity was performed by the applicant(s).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: See MPEP §715.01(d). Distinguish whether the activity constitutes a statutory bar and whether required acts occurred in a qualifying country under 37 CFR 1.131(a)(1) and 35 U.S.C. 104.

rubrics_metrics.name: How much of the claimed invention must be shown (commensurate possession)
rubrics_metrics.description: A 37 CFR 1.131 affidavit/declaration must establish possession of either the whole claimed invention or something falling within the claim (e.g., a species of a claimed genus) such that the claim as a whole reads on it; where differences are very small and treated by the examiner as obvious modifications, the affidavit need only show no more than the reference shows.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Cites In re Tanczyn (must read on the claim), In re Stryker, In re Wakefield, In re Spiller. Affidavit need not show identical disclosure but must show completion of the invention commensurate with the extent of the invention as claimed. If affiant’s showing is not fully commensurate, applicant may still overcome by showing that differences would have been obvious to one skilled in the art in view of applicant’s evidence. Ensure affidavit establishes possession of the basic inventive concept, not merely what a single reference happens to show.

rubrics_metrics.name: Swearing behind one of a plurality of combined references (antidating combinations)
rubrics_metrics.description: Applicant may overcome a 35 U.S.C. 103 rejection based on a combination of references by showing completion of the invention prior to the effective date of any of the references; it is not necessary to antedate the earliest filing date among combined references.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Even if relying on antedating one reference, the affidavit must show possession of the claimed invention prior to the effective date of the reference being antedated. Applicant can rely on teachings of a secondary reference to show that differences would have been obvious prior to the date of a later reference, but the 1.131 affidavit must still establish possession of the claimed invention (not just what Reference A shows) if Reference A does not teach the basic inventive concept. See related cases and discussion in text.

rubrics_metrics.name: General rule regarding generic claims (species antedating genus)
rubrics_metrics.description: In most cases, a reference or activity applied against generic claims may be antedated by an affidavit/declaration showing completion of only a single species within the genus prior to the effective date of the reference or activity (so long as the reference/activity is not a statutory bar or a patent/application publication claiming the same invention).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Cites Ex parte Biesecker, In re Fong, In re Defano. Exception: unpredictable arts — see MPEP §715.03 for practice in unpredictable arts where single species may not suffice; consider whether showing is commensurate with minimum patent specification support for a genus claim.

rubrics_metrics.name: Genus-species and predictability (when species proof insufficient)
rubrics_metrics.description: Where predictability is in question (unpredictable arts), an affidavit/declaration showing prior completion of one or a few species within a disclosed genus will generally not overcome a reference or activity that discloses a genus; the affidavit must show at least the minimum disclosure required by a patent specification to support a generic claim.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Apply tests from In re Shokal, Mantell, Rainer, DeFano, Clarke, Schaub. The number of species needed to infer genus possession depends on genus size (e.g., for small genus like halogens, reduction to practice of three species — perhaps two — might suffice; for large genera many more species may be required). The practical test is whether facts would persuade one skilled in the art that the applicant possessed as much of the invention as is shown in the reference or activity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Who may make an affidavit or declaration under 37 CFR 1.131
rubrics_metrics.description: Permitted declarants include (A) all the inventors of the claimed subject matter; (B) fewer than all named inventors when it is shown they invented the subject matter of the rejected claim(s); (C) a 37 CFR legal representative in situations where a petition under 37 CFR 1.47 was granted or application accepted under 1.42/1.43; (D) the assignee or other party in interest when the inventor’s affidavit/declaration cannot be produced; (E) the owner of the patent under reexamination.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Affidavits/declarations to overcome a rejection must be made by inventor(s) or an authorized party (37 CFR 1.42/1.43/1.47) or assignee/party in interest when inventor’s affidavit cannot be produced, or owner under reexamination. If one or more named inventors are unavailable to sign, remaining joint inventors may sign provided a petition under 37 CFR 1.183 requesting waiver of signature of the unavailable inventor is submitted with the affidavit/declaration and appropriate proof of unavailability is provided (similar to petition under 37 CFR 1.47). Petitions under 1.183 are decided by Office of Petitions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Formal requirements of affidavits and declarations
rubrics_metrics.description: An affidavit is a written statement made under oath before an authorized officer. 37 CFR 1.68 permits use of a declaration instead of an affidavit; the declaration must include an acknowledgment that willful false statements are punishable under 18 U.S.C. 1001 and a statement that statements of personal knowledge are true and statements on information and belief are believed to be true.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: See MPEP §§604–604.06 for formal affidavit requirements. Ensure required acknowledgements are present in declarations used in lieu of affidavits per 37 CFR 1.68, and that the declarant properly attests to truthfulness and understanding of criminal penalties.

rubrics_metrics.name: U.S. patent or application publication claiming same invention — remedies and limits of 1.131
rubrics_metrics.description: When a noncommonly owned U.S. patent or application publication claims the same invention and its publication/issue date is within specified timeframes relative to presentation of claims, the remedy may be interference (37 CFR 41.202) rather than 37 CFR 1.131; 35 U.S.C. 135(b)(1) or (b)(2) may require ex parte rejection depending on dates. A 37 CFR 1.131 affidavit is ineffective to overcome a U.S. patent or application publication that claims the same invention or that is not patentably distinct from the application’s claims.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If the reference publication date is less than one year prior to presentation of claims, applicant’s remedy, if any, is via interference (37 CFR 41.202) rather than 1.131. If a U.S. patent issues more than one year before presentation of claims to that invention, reject under 35 U.S.C. 135(b)(1). For commonly owned references where claims are not identical but not patentably distinct, a terminal disclaimer and an affidavit/declaration under 37 CFR 1.130 may be used to overcome a 35 U.S.C. 103 rejection. Use form paragraphs 23.14/23.14.01 for 35 U.S.C. 135(b) rejections. Cites In re McGrew and a line of cases (In re Clark, In re Hidy, etc.) holding 1.131 ineffective where there is no patentable distinction.
